Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Omar had always considered himself a man of quiet conviction. At fifty-six, he had built a life around stability: a long, loving marriage to his wife, Layla; a successful career as a social media manager for a non-profit; and a deep pride in his own resilience. That was before the night, six months ago, when his world fractured. Driving home from a community meeting, he was pulled over. The flashing lights in his rearview mirror were the first spark of an unease that quickly became a blaze of terror. It was a case of mistaken identity, they said later, but not before two officers had dragged him from his car, shouting commands he couldn't process fast enough. He remembered the rough scrape of asphalt against his cheek and the coppery taste of blood and dirt filling his mouth as his face was pushed into the pavement. What haunted him most was the sound of his own voice, pleading in a way he had never imagined he would. It felt like a betrayal of everything he thought he was.

In the months that followed, the man Layla knew began to disappear. The trauma didn't live in the past; it was a constant, predatory presence. A police siren wailing down the street would send a jolt through him, and for a split second, he could taste the grit of the pavement on his tongue again. The memory would start to unspool—the blinding headlights, the rough hands—but he would slam a mental door on it before it could take full shape, a desperate act of self-preservation that left him breathless and shaking. When a fragment did break through, it wasn't fear that seized him, but a white-hot rage that felt so vast it could swallow him whole. He began to believe the world was simply a dangerous place, and that any sense of safety was an illusion. People, he decided, were not what they seemed; a uniform or a friendly smile could hide anything.

His work, once a source of purpose, became a minefield. As a social media manager, he was required to be online, to engage with the world’s unfolding story. But he found himself unable to look at trending topics, terrified of stumbling upon a video of another traffic stop, another act of violence. He would spend hours meticulously curating his feeds to create a sterile, emotionless space, deleting any post that might evoke a strong feeling, good or bad. He just wanted to feel nothing. At the office, he couldn't sit in the open-plan space without his back to a solid wall. Before any meeting, he would instinctively locate the nearest two exits, his mind mapping escape routes before he could even register the agenda. He was in a state of constant, humming vigilance, scanning every room, every face, for threats he couldn't name. He knew, logically, that he was safe in his office or his own home, but his body refused to believe it. He could not relax.

This new reality bled into his home life. He stopped watching the evening news with Layla, then action movies, then eventually any drama at all. The risk of seeing something that would echo his experience was too great. He felt a deep, abiding shame about how he had acted that night, certain he had failed some fundamental test of character. This conviction made him withdraw, believing he was no longer the man his wife had married. He avoided family dinners and celebrations, the potential for joy feeling as threatening as the potential for pain. The emotional flatness he cultivated as a shield was becoming a prison, and the silence between him and Layla grew heavier each day. It was a warning from his manager about his declining performance at work that finally broke through his paralysis. He was told his disengagement was becoming a serious problem. The thought of losing his job, the last pillar of the life he once knew, was terrifying. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, afraid that the man he used to be was gone for good, but willing to try anything to find him again.
